title: Generative AI
description: The umbrella track tying together GANs, VAEs, diffusion models, and modern generative systems.
blurb: The umbrella track tying together GANs, VAEs, diffusion models, and modern generative systems.
careerApplications: Generative AI is the fastest-growing area of AI hiring; understanding the landscape across model families (not just LLMs) is what separates a generalist AI engineer from a prompt-only user.

advanced: Production use cases & choosing the right model family

lessons.title: What generative AI is
objectives: Define generative AI and name its major output types
Explain how generative vs discriminative changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect generative vs discriminative with content creation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Generative AI creates NEW content — text, images, audio, video — rather than just labeling or predicting a category on existing content. A spam filter is discriminative (sorts existing emails); an LLM writing an email, or a diffusion model painting an image from a text prompt, is generative (creates something new that didn't exist before).
examples:
# discriminative: given an email, predict spam/not-spam (a label for existing input)
# generative: given a prompt, produce a brand-new email/image/song that didn't exist before
commonMistakes: Treating 'generative AI' as synonymous with 'LLMs' — image generation (GANs/diffusion), audio generation, and video generation are all equally generative AI, built on different underlying.
lessons.careerRelevance: This distinction is the entry point to understanding the whole landscape, not just the chatbot part of it.

lessons.title: Generative vs discriminative models
objectives: Contrast what each model type learns and is used for
Explain how decision boundary changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect decision boundary with data distribution and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A discriminative model learns a decision boundary — 'given X, what's the most likely label Y' — directly, often with less data needed for that narrow task.
examples:
# discriminative: P(label | image) -- 'is this a cat?'
# generative: P(image) -- 'what does a realistic cat image look like, generally?'
# a generative model COULD be used to classify too, but that's not its main strength
commonMistakes: Assuming a generative model is always the 'better' or 'more advanced' choice — for a pure classification task with plenty of labels, a simpler discriminative model is usually more accurate.
lessons.careerRelevance: This framing is exactly what interviewers use to test whether you understand WHY each model family exists.

lessons.title: Probability distributions & sampling
objectives: Explain what 'sampling from a distribution' means for a generative model
Explain how probability distribution changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect probability distribution with sampling and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Every generative model, in some form, learns a probability distribution over its output space, then SAMPLES from it to produce something new.
examples:
# a trained model doesn't memorize ONE image of a cat --
# it learns a distribution over 'realistic cat images'
# and each generation is one random SAMPLE from that distribution

lessons.title: Latent representations & major model families
objectives: Describe what a latent space is and name the major generative model families
Explain how latent space changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect latent space with GANs vs VAEs vs diffusion vs transformers and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A latent space is a compressed, lower-dimensional representation of the data's essential features — a way of describing 'what makes this image/text distinct' in far fewer numbers than the raw pixels/tokens.
examples:
# same underlying idea, different mechanisms:
# GAN: generator tries to fool a discriminator
# VAE: encode to a latent distribution, decode back, sampled probabilistically
# Diffusion: learn to remove noise, step by step
# Transformer/LLM: predict the next token given context
concepts: GANs vs VAEs vs diffusion vs transformers

lessons.title: Training vs inference, prompting & conditioning
objectives: Distinguish training-time and inference-time, and explain conditioning
Explain how training vs inference changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect training vs inference with conditioning and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Training is the (expensive, one-time-ish) process of learning the distribution from data. Inference is using the trained model to generate new outputs — cheap, per-request.
examples:
# training: learn from millions of (image, caption) pairs -- expensive, done once (or periodically)
# inference: 'generate an image of a red bicycle' -- cheap, done per request
# the caption/prompt is the CONDITIONING signal steering what gets generated
commonMistakes: Confusing fine-tuning (updating model weights, a training-time activity) with prompting (steering a fixed model at inference time, no weight changes) — they solve similar problems very.
lessons.careerRelevance: This distinction underlies every practical decision about cost, speed, and customization in a real generative AI product.

lessons.title: Evaluation, hallucination & reliability
objectives: Explain why evaluating generative models is uniquely hard, and what hallucination means
Explain how evaluation difficulty changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect evaluation difficulty with hallucination and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Unlike classification, there's often no single 'correct' output to check against — many different generated images or sentences could all be 'good.' This makes evaluation genuinely hard, often requiring human judgment or proxy metrics.
examples:
# no single 'correct answer' to check against, unlike a classification label
# proxy metrics exist (e.g. FID for images, perplexity for text)
# but human evaluation is still often necessary for real quality judgment
commonMistakes: Assuming a confident-sounding or good-looking generated output is necessarily correct — confidence and correctness are not the same thing for generative models, ever.
lessons.careerRelevance: Reliability and hallucination are now central, explicit concerns in every real generative AI product decision, not an academic footnote.

lessons.title: Risk: copyright, bias, privacy & misuse
objectives: Identify the major categories of risk generative AI systems raise
Explain how copyright provenance changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect copyright provenance with bias amplification and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Generative models trained on large scraped datasets raise real, unresolved questions: copyright (was training on this data legal/licensed, and who owns generated output that resembles it), bias (models reproduce and can amplify biases present in training data), privacy (models can sometimes memorize and regurgitate sensitive training examples).
examples:
# real, ongoing categories of concern:
# copyright -- training data provenance, output ownership
# bias -- reproducing/amplifying training-data biases
# privacy -- memorized sensitive training examples resurfacing
# misuse -- deepfakes, impersonation, disinformation at scale
commonMistakes: Treating these risks as someone else's problem ('the model vendor handles that') — anyone building a product on top of generative AI inherits real responsibility for how it's used and what.
lessons.careerRelevance: These are now standard, expected discussion topics in generative AI interviews and product reviews, not a specialist ethics-only concern.
lessons.explain: Generative models trained on large scraped datasets raise real, unresolved questions: copyright (was training on this data legal/licensed, and who owns generated output that resembles it), bias (models reproduce and can amplify biases present in training data), privacy (models can sometimes memorize and regurgitate sensitive training examples).

lessons.title: Production use cases & choosing the right model family
objectives: Match a real use case to the right generative model family
Explain how model family selection changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect model family selection with use-case fit and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Putting it together: text generation/chat -> transformers/LLMs; photorealistic image generation -> diffusion models (current state of the art); fast, real-time image synthesis or when you need an easily-manipulable latent space -> GANs or VAEs depending on the need; structured latent-space exploration or anomaly detection -> VAEs specifically.

# 'realistic', highest current quality images -> diffusion
# fast/real-time image generation, adversarial training tolerance -> GANs
# need a smooth, structured latent space to interpolate/explore -> VAEs
# any text generation/chat/reasoning task -> transformers/LLMs

lessons.title: Prompting as the primary interface
objectives: Explain why prompting became the dominant way to interact with generative models
Explain how prompting as interface changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect prompting as interface with natural language control and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Unlike traditional software with fixed APIs, many generative models are controlled almost entirely through natural-language prompts -- the prompt itself becomes the 'interface' shaping behavior, tone, and output format, without writing code for each new task.
examples:
# same model, different prompts = different tasks:
# 'Summarize this in one sentence' vs 'List 3 risks in this text'
# no new code, no retraining -- just a different instruction
commonMistakes: Assuming a generative model needs custom code for every new task, when often a well-written prompt alone can redirect its behavior.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding prompting as the primary control surface is foundational to working with any modern generative system.

quiz.q: A generative model's core goal is to:
options: classify existing inputs
learn a distribution and sample new outputs from it
only compress data
only detect anomalies

quiz.q: Hallucination in generative AI refers to:
options: a hardware failure
confidently generating false or fabricated content
a training crash
a type of data augmentation

quiz.q: Prompting a fixed pretrained model is best described as:
options: training-time weight updates
an inference-time conditioning signal
a type of GAN loss
irrelevant to generative AI

quiz.q: For the highest-quality photorealistic image generation today, the dominant approach is:
options: GANs exclusively
VAEs exclusively
diffusion models
decision trees

quiz.q: Model bias in generative AI mainly comes from:
options: random hardware noise
patterns present in the training data
the programming language used
the size of the output image

quiz.q: What is the key difference between generative and discriminative models?
options: they're identical
generative models create new content resembling training data; discriminative models predict a label or decision boundary
discriminative models are always more accurate
generative models never use training data

quiz.q: What does P(Y|X) represent in a discriminative model?
options: the probability of generating new data
the probability of a label Y given input X
the total dataset size
a synonym for sampling

quiz.q: What does sampling from a probability distribution let a generative model do?
options: produce the exact same output every time
produce varied, plausible outputs rather than one deterministic answer
only work with text data
skip training entirely

quiz.q: What is a latent space?
options: the raw training dataset
a compressed, learned representation of data that a generative model can navigate to produce outputs
a synonym for a loss function
the model's file size

quiz.q: What model families does 'GANs vs VAEs vs diffusion vs transformers' broadly categorize?
options: types of databases
major distinct architectural approaches to generative modeling
evaluation metrics only
types of loss functions

quiz.q: What is the difference between training and inference for a generative model?
options: they're identical processes
training learns the model's parameters from data; inference uses the already-trained model to generate new output
inference always takes longer than training
training happens after inference

quiz.q: What role does a prompt play during inference?
options: it retrains the model
it acts as a conditioning signal, steering what the model generates without changing its underlying weights
prompts are irrelevant during inference
prompts only work during training

quiz.q: What is hallucination, in generative AI?
options: a hardware malfunction
a model confidently producing false or fabricated information as if it were true
a synonym for training
a type of data augmentation

quiz.q: Why is evaluating generative model output often harder than evaluating a classifier?
options: it isn't harder
there's often no single 'correct' output, unlike a classifier's clear right/wrong label, making automated evaluation trickier
classifiers have no evaluation methods
generative models can't be evaluated at all

quiz.q: Why do proxy metrics for generative quality sometimes diverge from real human judgment?
options: they never diverge
an automated metric can score well while a human still finds the output subtly wrong or unhelpful
human judgment is always identical to automated scores
proxy metrics are always more reliable

quiz.q: What is data memorization, as a generative AI risk?
options: a performance optimization
a model reproducing specific training examples too closely, raising privacy or copyright concerns
a synonym for hallucination
a required training step

quiz.q: Why is copyright provenance a real concern for generative models?
options: copyright never applies to AI-generated content
training data or generated output may closely resemble copyrighted material without clear rights to use or reproduce it
provenance only matters for text, not images
this concern is purely theoretical with no real cases

quiz.q: What does bias amplification mean in generative AI?
options: the model becomes unbiased over time automatically
biases present in training data can be reflected or even exaggerated in generated outputs
bias only affects discriminative models
amplification refers to audio processing only

quiz.q: Why does misuse potential matter when releasing a generative model?
options: misuse is not a real concern
the same generative capability that enables helpful use cases can also enable harmful ones (deepfakes, spam, disinformation)
misuse only applies to open-source models
generative models can't be misused by design

quiz.q: What factors typically drive choosing between different generative model families for production?
options: only the model's name
quality vs speed vs control trade-offs specific to the use case
always pick the newest model regardless of fit
cost is never a factor

quiz.q: Why might a faster, lower-quality model be the right production choice over a slower, higher-quality one?
options: speed is always irrelevant
some use cases genuinely need low latency more than maximum quality, making the trade-off worthwhile
faster models are always higher quality too
this trade-off doesn't exist in practice

quiz.q: What output modalities can generative AI produce, beyond text?
options: only text
images, audio, video, and code, among other modalities
only numbers
only structured data tables

quiz.q: Why is stochasticity (randomness) often intentional in generative model outputs?
options: it's always a bug
controlled randomness lets the same prompt produce varied, creative outputs rather than one rigid answer every time
stochastic output is always undesirable
models must be fully deterministic to work

quiz.q: What does 'content creation' as generative AI's core capability refer to?
options: only classifying existing content
producing new content (text, images, etc.) resembling patterns learned from training data
deleting existing content
organizing files

quiz.q: Why is human review still often necessary even with capable generative models?
options: human review is never necessary anymore
models can hallucinate, encode bias, or miss context in ways that still require human judgment before real-world use
generative models are always perfectly accurate
review only matters for image generation

quiz.q: What is a decision boundary, in the context of discriminative models?
options: a type of generative output
the boundary a model learns to separate different classes/labels from each other
a synonym for latent space
a training hyperparameter only

quiz.q: Why can't proxy metrics alone fully replace human judgment when evaluating generated content?
options: proxy metrics are always sufficient
they can miss nuanced quality issues (tone, subtle inaccuracy, appropriateness) that a human evaluator would catch
human judgment is always less reliable
proxy metrics measure the exact same thing as human judgment

quiz.q: What does 'use-case fit' mean when choosing a model family?
options: always choosing the largest model available
matching a model family's actual strengths to what the specific task actually needs
fit refers only to file size compatibility
use-case fit is not a real consideration

quiz.q: Why might data provenance tracking matter for a company deploying generative AI?
options: provenance has no practical importance
understanding what data trained a model helps assess copyright, bias, and compliance risk before deployment
provenance only matters for open-source models
tracking provenance is technically impossible

quiz.q: What is the relationship between prompting and conditioning in generative models?
options: they are unrelated concepts
a prompt is one common way to condition (steer) what a generative model produces, without retraining it
conditioning requires retraining the model each time
prompting only applies to classification tasks
